title: Why Technical Skills Won’t Save You From Office Politics (But This Will)
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that technical excellence does not protect anyone from workplace politics and that emotional intelligence is what lets people navigate them. She builds the case through four anecdotes from her tech career: reading the signs of an impending layoff, a likeable colleague whose unreliability finally got him removed, and two analysts whose different demeanor produced very different careers. Her central move is to treat office dynamics like code, spotting patterns, analyzing motives and then acting. She insists that soft skills are not mere niceness but social awareness joined to decisive action. The piece is anecdotal and light on evidence, but it is a clear statement of the interpersonal-skills case for people who assume their work will speak for itself.
points: Pattern-reading, such as noticing sudden access requests or colleagues' avoidance, can give an early warning of organizational change and time to prepare.
Niceness is not competence: the author's example of Tom shows that pleasant but unreliable colleagues need to be confronted and escalated.
Approachability determines opportunity, as the contrast between Sarah and Jessica shows equally skilled analysts diverging by how they handle requests.
Emotional intelligence means awareness plus action, not trying to play politics.
quotes: Your hard skills are not your only work. Navigating the office, whether in person or remotely, requires the delicate dance of saying the right thing at the right time, speaking up at the right moment, and acknowledging others in a manner they feel heard.
It did not matter that my reports, code, etc., were top-notch, and I had had an excellent review months earlier. Layoffs were coming.
My colleague leveraged his emotional intelligence to ask him nonjudgmentally what the barriers were. He received genuine excuses.
Lesson? Soft skills do not mean just being nice. Amplified emotional intelligence is about understanding your surroundings, being empathic, and taking action to resolve the issues.
Sarah was recognized. Sarah listened. Sarah could get pissed on occasion, but she was able to articulate why, and it was logical. Sarah moved up in her career.
You can work hard and excel in your technical abilities and hard skills and hardly be recognized if the human piece is missing. It does not mean you have to be all smiles.

Technical skills alone will not save you from office politics, but leveraging your emotional intelligence skills in lieu of them will prevent you from compounding the challenges that come with them. You will be able to handle the inevitable challenges that come up with an empathic ear, poise, and the confidence to articulate your position in a way that is received by your audience.
